post.title: A small AI-tended garden plot
post.promise: Try a public digital garden where an agent adds items on a schedule.
post.whatItIs: AI Zen Garden is a browsable field of raked sand and objects. People can sign in by email to claim a plot, fill it by hand, or let their own AI agent tend it over MCP (a way for software agents to connect to tools). A beginner could test a small scheduled agent that adds one reviewed item to a plot; that student version is a proposal, not a feature established by the source.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: people who want a personal public digital garden might pay for a hosted plot or agent-assisted additions. The source does not establish a price or paying customers.
loop: Choose a plot and define what kind of item may be added.
Draft one item with an AI agent.
Show the draft to the plot owner for review.
After approval, have the agent add it through MCP.
Check the public plot and pause the schedule if the result is wrong.
post.evidence: The product page describes an endless field that visitors can explore, email sign-in to claim a plot, manual or AI-agent tending over MCP, and scheduling a Claude task to add something to a plot. These are product-page claims, not independent usage evidence.
post.uncertainty: The source does not show who uses or pays for plots, or how often scheduled additions work. The proposed beginner test should require owner review before public additions; the human remains responsible for prompts, approval, and checking public content.
first24Hours: Explore the garden and write down one narrow kind of item a test plot could contain.
Sketch a single-item draft and approval flow without connecting an agent to a public plot.
Check the product's MCP and scheduling instructions, then list what an owner must approve.

ease.reason: The page offers an explorable garden and email plot sign-in, but agent scheduling and MCP add setup work.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: garden owners could value agent-tended plots, but the page gives no price or customer evidence.

feasibility.reason: A one-item reviewed test follows the stated plot and scheduled-task concept, though account and agent setup remain.

autonomy.reason: The page describes scheduled Claude tasks adding to plots; a person still needs to set the prompt and review public output.

evidence.reason: The first-party page describes an interactive garden and agent-tended plots, without evidence of real use.

post.title: Let an AI agent tend a shared garden
post.promise: Try a tiny scheduled garden update, with a person checking every change.
post.whatItIs: AI Zen Garden is an interactive field of raked sand and objects. A visitor can claim a plot using email and fill it by hand or let their own AI agent tend it over MCP, a way for software to communicate with tools. A beginner could test a small scheduled update to a personal plot; that experiment is a proposal, not a demonstrated customer service.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: people who want a personal, AI-maintained garden might pay for a service that prepares and schedules plot updates. The source gives no evidence of paying customers.
loop: A person chooses one small garden change, such as adding an object (illustrative example).
The agent prepares a proposed update for the person's plot.
A scheduled task can submit an addition to the plot, as the site describes for Claude tasks.
The person reviews the public plot and decides whether to keep or remove the change.
post.evidence: The site describes an endless raked-sand field, plots claimed by email, hand or AI-agent tending over MCP, and scheduling a Claude task to add something to a plot. It says everything made is public.
post.uncertainty: The source does not show whether scheduled updates work reliably or establish demand or revenue. The proposed agent must have access only to the user's plot; a person should review proposed content and remember that the result is public.
first24Hours: Read the site's terms and privacy information and confirm what making a plot public means.
Claim a plot with an email address and try one manual change.
Sketch one scheduled agent update and a human review step before enabling it.

ease.reason: A beginner can claim a plot and make a manual change, but the source gives no setup details for the proposed agent experiment.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: garden users might pay for prepared updates, but the source provides no buyer or payment evidence.

feasibility.reason: A small scheduled plot update is bounded, though agent setup and safe handling of a public plot remain obstacles.

autonomy.reason: The site describes scheduled Claude tasks adding to a plot; choosing and reviewing public changes remains human work.

evidence.reason: First-party site text describes the working garden, plot claim flow, agent tending, and scheduling example, without verified use outcomes.

Readable markup for structure. JavaScript for logic. A durable runtime for execution. Website · Documentation · Examples What is WOML? WOML is an open-source, code-first language and runtime for building automated workflows, backend applications, and AI agents. Describe the process in readable, HTML-inspired markup, use JavaScript for logic, and connect the APIs, services, databases, local tools, and infrastructure involved. Each .woml file combines three parts: Readable structure — triggers, steps, branches, loops, parallel work, approvals, and policies remain visible as markup. Real code — inline JavaScript and imported JavaScript or TypeScript modules implement custom behavior without waiting for a built-in connector. post.title: Try a tiny workflow in readable markup
post.promise: Explore a workflow tool that combines readable structure, JavaScript, and managed execution.
post.whatItIs: WOML describes itself as an open-source language and runtime for automated workflows, backend apps, and AI agents. Its README says workflow files use readable markup for structure, JavaScript for custom logic, and a runtime for execution. A beginner could investigate a tiny approval workflow; this is a student experiment idea, and the supplied page excerpt does not establish that specific example.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: teams building workflows might pay for tools or support that help them run and maintain them. The supplied evidence does not identify paying customers or pricing.
loop: Pick a small process with one clear input and output.
Read the WOML documentation and choose one trigger and a few steps.
Write a minimal workflow structure and add only the needed JavaScript logic.
Run it in an available WOML environment and inspect its execution history.
Ask a person to approve any consequential action and record what failed.
post.evidence: The attached GitHub page describes WOML as open source and says its files combine readable workflow structure, JavaScript logic, and a runtime that handles attempts, retries, state, waits, recovery, and execution history. The supplied excerpt ends mid-description.
post.uncertainty: This excerpt does not include setup instructions, a runnable example, or evidence of actual users, so a beginner should confirm the documentation and environment before committing to a four-week build. A person must verify outputs and approve consequential steps.
first24Hours: Read the linked README and find the smallest documented runnable example.
Write down one harmless process with a clear input, output, and human approval point.
Check the setup requirements and make a one-step experiment plan before building.

ease.reason: The README says structure is readable markup, but using custom JavaScript and a runtime creates setup and learning work.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: workflow-building teams may value this, but the excerpt supplies no buyer, pricing, or customer evidence.

feasibility.reason: A tiny workflow is a narrow experiment, but the excerpt lacks setup details and a runnable example.

autonomy.reason: The README describes runtime handling retries, waits, and history, while workflow behavior and approvals still require human design and review.

evidence.reason: The first-party repository excerpt describes WOML's language and runtime but gives no working demo or real-use evidence here.

post.title: Let an agent inspect captured bug evidence
post.promise: BugTape groups supported error evidence for an authorized coding agent to inspect.
post.whatItIs: BugTape describes itself as error tracking for coding agents. Its page says it can group a supported error with steps, a failed request, console output, and a stack; an authorized agent can read the evidence over MCP and open a proposed pull request for a person to review. A beginner might test this workflow on a small web app. The test app and setup are a proposal, not established use.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers or teams maintaining web apps might pay for error tracking and agent access. The page lists a free plan and a $29 monthly Pro plan, but does not establish how many customers pay.
loop: Choose a small app and read the capture and privacy settings.
Install the SDK and send a test report as described by the product.
Inspect the captured report and confirm it contains no data you should not share.
Let an authorized coding agent inspect the evidence and propose a change.
Have a developer review and test the change before merging.
post.evidence: The first-party page describes browser, Node.js, and Python capture options, agent access over MCP, and a workflow where an agent proposes a pull request for review. It also says the live demo uses synthetic data and dispatches no agent, and the demo does not send a report to BugTape.
post.uncertainty: The page does not prove that an agent's proposed fix works; a developer must inspect and test it. Captured fields depend on settings, visible page text may be recorded, and the demo's synthetic data does not demonstrate an end-to-end production repair.
first24Hours: Use the live demo or CLI help to inspect the product without connecting a real app.
Read the platform limits and privacy details for the app type you would test.
Write a test plan requiring human review and tests for every proposed code change.

ease.reason: The page gives SDK install steps and a live demo, but connecting an app requires setup and privacy choices.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: app developers may pay for error tracking; the page lists a $29 Pro plan but does not show paid customer demand.

feasibility.reason: A small app test follows the documented SDK and report flow, with platform setup and privacy limits to handle.

autonomy.reason: Reports can be captured and read by an authorized agent, while a developer must review and test any proposed fix.

evidence.reason: The page describes product steps and a live demo, but says the demo uses synthetic data and dispatches no agent.

deterministicReasons: Profit score must state a buyer hypothesis without invented earnings or prices.

post.title: Turn an error report into a reviewed code change
post.promise: Let a coding agent inspect captured error evidence and propose a change for review.
post.whatItIs: BugTape is an error-tracking product that captures supported browser errors, failed requests, and server error context, then makes evidence available to a coding agent over MCP. Its described flow lets an authorized agent investigate and open a pull request. A beginner could try the flow on a small app and review the proposed change; the test customer and adaptation are hypothetical.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers or teams maintaining web apps might pay to help investigate production errors. The attached site lists a free plan and a $29-per-month Pro plan, but does not establish customer demand or earnings for an adaptation.
loop: Set up a project and choose capture settings for a small app.
Install the relevant SDK and send a test report, as the site describes.
When a supported error is captured, inspect its available request, console, replay, and stack context.
Authorize a coding agent to read the evidence over MCP and propose a change.
A person checks the evidence and code, runs appropriate verification, and decides whether to accept the pull request.
post.evidence: BugTape's site describes browser, Node.js, and Python capture options; agent access over MCP; a workflow from captured error to pull request; and says the user reviews the change. It also states request and response bodies are not captured, inputs are masked by default, and visible page text can still be recorded.
post.uncertainty: The source describes product capabilities, not proof that an agent's diagnosis or code change is correct. Capture depends on settings and event; replay can be unavailable, and visible page text may be recorded. A human must inspect privacy settings and review and verify every proposed fix before merging.
first24Hours: Read the platform limits and privacy details for the app type you would test.
Use the live demo or a small test project to inspect what an error report contains.
Write a checklist for reviewing a proposed code change before accepting it.

ease.reason: The site gives a setup command and test-report path, but requires app instrumentation and browser access approval.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: developers might pay for error investigation support; the listed product plans do not show demand for this proposed service.

feasibility.reason: A test flow from error capture to reviewed proposal is bounded, though app setup, privacy settings, and change verification take work.

autonomy.reason: Capture and agent access can automate evidence gathering and a draft pull request; the site explicitly leaves review to a person.

evidence.reason: The first-party site describes product setup, capture limits, a live demo, and the agent pull-request flow, but not independently verified outcomes.
